newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS - Lufthansa dives on share ownership limits.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Lufthansa dives on share ownership limits.

text.p: Shares in Deutsche Lufthansa AG plunged by as much five percent on Tuesday as the German government stunned international investors with a draft law imposing limits on foreign ownership in the airline.

Lufthansa stock dived 1.25 marks to a low of 20.60 after the Transport Ministry proposed measures to restrict foreign ownership of the airline to 50 percent, in preparation for the flotation of the state's remaining 36 percent stake this year.
The restrictions are standard for airlines and are required by international air laws which demand that flag carriers have domestic ownership.

But Frankfurt share dealers said investors had been scared by clauses requiring Lufthansa ordinary shares to be converted to stock with restricted transfer rights, and giving Lufthansa the right in certain cases to force foreign investors to sell their shares.
"The whole deal is making people less sure of the company," said one equities trader.
But airline analysts said the panic was overdone and that the experience of other privatised flag carriers showed the risk of compulsory share repurchases was not great.

"People are over-reacting to the risk of forced sales. In 10 years, British Airways has not got close to its limit (setting out similar foreign ownership restrictions)," Dresdner Kleinwort Benson analyst Chris Tarry said.
Tarry said British Airways currently had foreign ownership of around 23 percent, comparable to the estimated 20 percent international shareholding base in Lufthansa.

The German Transport Ministry said later at news conference that any share repurchases would in any case be carried out on a "last in, first out" basis, meaning that existing investors faced no risk of being forced to relinquish their stakes.

Lufthansa itself welcomed the draft law as an "appropriate measure" and said it paved the way for the sale of Bonn's remaining stake, worth some three billion marks, around the fourth quarter of this year.

A spokesman said that, assuming the law was passed in the coming months, Lufthansa shareholders would be called on to approve the possible implications for its shares at a meeting to be held in late-June.

The Transport Ministry said that from this March, a computer-based trading system would be available for non-freely transferable shares that would allow them to be traded "as easily and reliably as ordinary shares".

Some of the shares in German reinsurance giant Munich Re, another stock in the DAX-30 top German share index, also carry transfer restrictions, as is common in the German insurance sector for reasons of share ownership control.

In Lufthansa's case, if more than 40 percent of its shares fell into foreign hands, it would then be allowed to buy back its own stock. If the proportion rose above 45 percent, a new share issue in which existing shareholders would not be allowed to take part would be possible.
In the extreme case that foreign shareholders gain more than 50 percent of the airline's shares, it would be permitted to force foreign shareholders to sell their stock.
After their initial drop, Lufthansa stock pulled back from their lows to trade down 84 pfennigs at 21.01 marks at the end of bourse dealings.
